details:
**"Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short"**
Hobbes's famous description in Chapter 13 of the life of man in the state of nature, where there is no common power to keep people in awe. It is the most common giveaway for Leviathan.

**"War of every man against every man" (war of all against all)**
In the state of nature, without a sovereign, people are in constant war because of competition, diffidence (distrust), and glory. Hobbes argues that men are naturally equal, because despite differences in strength and craft, even the weakest can kill the strongest. The Latin phrase bellum omnium contra omnes is associated with this idea.

**"Of the Kingdom of Darkness"**
The fourth and final part of Leviathan. It attacks a "confederacy of deceivers," above all the Roman Catholic Church, who keep people in spiritual ignorance. It names four causes of this darkness: misinterpretation of Scripture, the demonology of the heathen poets, mixing Scripture with the vain philosophy of the Greeks (especially Aristotle), and false traditions. It calls the "main abuse" of Scripture the claim that the Kingdom of God is the present church.

**Abraham Bosse's frontispiece**
The famous title page, designed by Abraham Bosse, shows a giant crowned sovereign rising over a landscape and town. His body is made of many small people, and he holds a sword and a crozier, symbolizing civil and church power. Panels below show military and ecclesiastical emblems. The title refers to the sea monster in the Book of Job.

**"Artificial man" and the body politic**
The introduction calls the commonwealth, or state, an "artificial man," of greater stature and strength than the natural man, created by human art. It begins by saying that "life is but a motion of limbs," so automata may be said to have artificial life.

**Laws of nature**
In Chapters 14 and 15, Hobbes lists nineteen laws of nature, in contrast to the single "right of nature," which is the liberty to use any means to preserve oneself. The first law is "to seek peace, and follow it," the second is to give up one's right to all things if others do the same, and the third is that men keep the covenants they make. All are summed up in the dictum "Do not that to another, which thou wouldest not have done to thyselfe."

**Covenant and the twelve rights of the sovereign**
People escape the state of nature by a covenant in which each "authorizes" one person or assembly to act as the "author" of all their actions, creating the commonwealth. In Part II, "Of Commonwealth," Hobbes lists twelve principal rights of the sovereign, including judicial and law-making power. Subjects cannot change the form of government, since a later covenant cannot override the earlier one.

**No summum bonum; violent death as the greatest evil**
Hobbes denies that there is a summum bonum, a single greatest good or final end, that all people pursue. Instead, he treats violent death as the greatest evil (summum malum), and the fear of violent death drives people to seek peace and form a commonwealth.

**Four parts: "Of Man," "Of Commonwealth," "Of a Christian Commonwealth," "Of the Kingdom of Darkness"**
The structure of the book. Part III argues that religious authority must be subordinate to the civil sovereign. Its reasoning is that no one can know whether another person's claimed divine revelation is genuine, so Scripture is authoritative only as interpreted under the sovereign. It warns that dividing spiritual and temporal power makes people "see double."

**Three kinds of commonwealth**
Hobbes says there are only three forms of government: monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy. "Tyranny" and "oligarchy" are just names for monarchy and aristocracy that people dislike. He argues that monarchy is best at avoiding civil war.

**Vital and voluntary motion; appetite and aversion**
Chapter 6 divides animal motion into involuntary "vital" motions, such as breathing and circulation, and "voluntary" motions caused by the imagination. The passions are forms of appetite and aversion, and the will is defined as "the last appetite in deliberating."

**"Decaying sense" and the "train of thoughts"**
Hobbes defines imagination as "nothing but decaying sense." To illustrate the "train of thoughts," he describes a discussion of the civil war in which someone asked the value of a Roman penny. The question seemed random but was linked by association to the betrayal of Christ for thirty pence.

**Speech, reason, and the "four abuses" of speech**
In Part I, which is laid out almost like a geometric demonstration, Hobbes says speech exists to transfer mental discourse into verbal discourse. He lists four abuses of speech, defines reason as "reckoning" (adding and subtracting), and calls "incorporeal substance" a self-contradictory term. In a later appendix, he defended God's corporeality, partly in response to Bishop John Bramhall.

**The Fool: "there is no such thing as Justice"**
In Chapter 15, echoing Psalms 14:1, Hobbes answers "the fool" who "hath said in his heart, there is no such thing as justice" and that breaking covenants can be rational. Hobbes argues that keeping covenants is required by reason.

**Liberty as "absence of external impediments"**
Hobbes defines liberty as the absence of external impediments to motion. He says that the liberty of subjects in a commonwealth lies in the "silence of the law," meaning whatever the sovereign has not forbidden.
